account: On 24 October 2023, teams led by Zhao Guoguang (Xuanwu Hospital) and Hong Bo (Tsinghua University) implanted the NEO wireless epidural brain-computer interface. The patient was a 54-year-old man with complete C4 spinal cord injury (ASIA A) from a car accident, quadriplegic for 14 years. He was discharged ten days later and trained at home for three months. At a trial-phase summary meeting on 29 January 2024, the team reported that he could drive a pneumatic glove with his brain activity to drink water unaided, with grasp-decoding accuracy above 90%. The team also reported improved ASIA scores and somatosensory evoked potentials. In a preprint of September 2024, the authors reported nine months of home use. They reported a grasp-detection F1-score of 0.91, eating and drinking, and a gain of 27 points on the Action Research Arm Test. On 13 March 2026 Scientific American reported that China approved Neuracle's implant for commercial use in people with spinal cord injuries. It reported that the approval covers only people who still have some upper arm function.

ai_role.statement: The AI contribution is the decoder, a Riemannian-geometry classifier with a hidden Markov model for temporal smoothing. Calibrated in about ten minutes on beta, low-gamma and high-gamma features of eight-channel epidural ECoG, it detects grasp intention and triggers the pneumatic glove. The preprint reports 94% calibration accuracy and a grasp-detection F1-score rising above 0.9 after three months (average 0.91 over nine months). It gives 100% object-transfer success with the BCI against 35% without. The electrodes, implant, surgery and glove are not AI. The authors attribute the later neurological recovery to repeated BCI training, not the decoder alone.

fields.account: On 24 October 2023, teams led by Zhao Guoguang (Xuanwu Hospital) and Hong Bo (Tsinghua University) implanted the NEO wireless epidural brain-computer interface. The patient was a 54-year-old man with complete C4 spinal cord injury (ASIA A) from a car accident, quadriplegic for 14 years. He was discharged ten days later and trained at home for three months. At a trial-phase summary meeting on 29 January 2024, the team reported that he could drive a pneumatic glove with his brain activity to drink water unaided, with grasp-decoding accuracy above 90%. The team also reported improved ASIA scores and somatosensory evoked potentials. In a preprint of September 2024, the authors reported nine months of home use. They reported a grasp-detection F1-score of 0.91, eating and drinking, and a gain of 27 points on the Action Research Arm Test. On 13 March 2026 Scientific American reported that China approved Neuracle's implant for commercial use in people with spinal cord injuries. It reported that the approval covers only people who still have some upper arm function.
